paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
**********
Criminal Appeal No. 1771 of 2001
Sadda ...........Appellant

versus
State of Uttarakhand ......Respondent
Sri Karan Anand, Advocate for the appellant.
Sri P.S. Saun, A.G.A. and Ms. Meena Bohara Brief Holder for the State.

U.C. Dhyani, J. (Oral)
PW1 S.I. Yogendra Singh set the criminal law into
motion by lodging F.I.R. against accused-appellant on 2.12.97
at 8:15 P.M. in P.S. Vikasnagar, District Dehradun, which was
registered as case crime no. 508/97 under Sections 8/18/20 of
the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985.
228 grams of opium was found from the possession of the
accused-appellant on 2.12.97 at 5.30 P.M. The distance
between the place of incident and P.S. concerned was 04 kms.
Hence, there appears to be no delay in lodging F.I.R.
2. After the investigation, a charge sheet was submitted
against the accused. Before that, a report was obtained from
Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL), Agra, who affirmed the
presence of opium in the representative sample. When the trial
began and prosecution opened its' case, charge for the offence
punishable under Section 8/18 N.D.P.S. Act, 1895 was framed
against the accused, who pleaded not guilty to the charge and

2
claimed trial. PW1 S.I. Yogendra Singh, PW2 Constable
Jagdev Singh, PW3 Constable Prem Singh, PW4 S.I. Zakir
Hussain, PW5 Sri O.P. Taneja, Joint Director, FSL Agra, PW6
H.C. Gajraj Singh and PW7 Surendra Singh Bisht S.O. were
examined on behalf of the prosecution. Incriminating evidence
was put to the accused-appellant, who said that the prosecution
evidence was false and he was falsely implicated in the case.
No evidence was given in defence. After considering the
evidence on record, accused was found guilty of the offence
punishable under Section 8/18 of the N.D.P.S. Act, and was
sentenced appropriately, vide impugned judgment and order
dated 17.7.2001, passed by learned Sessions Judge, Dehradun.
Aggrieved against the impugned judgment and order, present
criminal appeal was preferred.
3. PW1 S.I. Yogendra Singh, in his examination in-chief,
said that he was on patrol duty alongwith other police
personnel, namely Head Constable Ranbir Singh, Constable
Lokendra and Constable Prem Singh on 2.12.97. At about 4.30
P.M., when they reached near bridge no. 2 of Shakti Canal, one
person was seen coming from the side of Dakpathar. That
person tried to move fast after looking at the police party.
Suspecting some foul, the police officials apprehended him at
about 5.30 P.M., 20 steps ahead of bridge no. 2. After taking
search of each other as per rules, a memo was prepared. The
accused was interrogated, who disclosed his name as Sadda,
son of Asgar. On being searched, 228 gms of opium was
recovered from his possession, which was sealed on the spot

3
according to rules and the accused was taken in police custody,
a memo of arrest and recovery memo was prepared and the
accused was brought at police station alongwith the recovered
contraband. The F.I.R. was lodged against the accused under
Sections 8/18/20 of the N.D.P.S. Act and the recovered
contraband was deposited at the police Station.
4. The prosecution led the evidence through PW1 S.I.
Yogendra Singh and PW 3 Constable Prem Singh. They said
that on 2.12.1997, the police personal headed by S.I. Yogendra
Singh and comprising of Head Constable Ranbir Singh and
Constables Lokendra Sing and Prem Singh were on patrol duty.
When they reached near bridge no. 2, they saw a person coming
from the side of Dakpathar. Seeing the police party, he tried to
run away. Suspecting some foul, he was apprehended by the
police at 5.30 P.M. 20 feet ahead of bridge No. 2. No public
witness could be procured in the jungle, as the same was a
lonely place. The police officials made a search of each other
according to rules and on being satisfied that none was having
any illegal article, a Memo Ext-Ka1 was prepared. On being
enquired, the accused disclosed his name as Sadda, son of
Asgar and on being searched, some black thing in a polythene
was recovered from his right pocket. It smelt opium. Visibly
also, the same was opium. Constable Lokendra Singh was sent
to bring weighing machine. He brought weighing machine from
Vikasnagar from the shop of Ram Kishan, a memo Ext-Ka2
whereof was prepared. The recovered contraband weighed 228
grams. Two samples of 4 grams each were kept in empty match

4
boxes and were sealed on the spot. The remaining contraband
was sealed in the same polythene from which it was recovered.
Sample of seal was also prepared. A memo of arrest and
recovery memo was given to the accused under his signature.
Ext-Ka3 (Memo of arrest) and recovery Memo alongwith other
papers Exts-Ka1 to Ka3 were proved by PW1 S.I. Yogendra
Singh. Both the witnesses stated that the accused and the
recovered articles in sealed condition were brought to the
Police Station, where the case crime was registered against the
accused and the contraband was deposited. Higher police
authorities were informed through wireless and the recovered
contraband was delivered to Head Constable Jagram. It was
also stated by PW1 S.I. Yogendra Singh and PW2 Jagdev
Singh that Constable Prem Singh was sent to the house of the
accused to give information about the recovery of opium from
the possession of the accused, vide Memo Ext-Ka4.
5. PW 2 Constable Jagdev Singh brought the sealed
contraband in the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate concerned
and then carried the same from the Court of Chief Judicial
Magistrate to FSL, Agra for chemical examination. He proved
Ext-Ka5, which was the letter written by Chief Judicial
Magistrate to Chemical Analyst, Agra. He stated that the
contraband was kept in sealed condition so long as the same
remained in his custody and nobody was allowed to touch the
same. He was cross-examined by the defence, but nothing
material could come out in his cross-examination to suspect
PW2's testimony.

5
6. PW 6 Head Constable Gajraj Singh proved chik F.I.R.
(Ext-Ka8) of this case, which was lodged on the basis of
recovery memo. The witness enterd the same in G.D. (Ext-Ka9). PW6 also filed and proved the copy of the G.D. showing
the departure of S.I. Yogendra Singh, Head Constable Randhir
Singh, Constable Prem Singh and Constable Lokendra Singh
from police station Vikas Nagar for patrol duty on 2.12.1997.
The copy of G.D. (Ext-Ka11) was on record. PW6 also proved
Ext-Ka12, regarding deposit of the recovered contraband by
S.I. Yogendra Singh in sealed condition at police station on
2.12.1997. He was also cross examined by the defence counsel,
but nothing material came in his cross-examination, which
might be of any benefit to the accused.
7. PW 7 S.O. Surendra Singh Bisht took up the
investigation of this case on 16.12.1997. He stated that the
recovered contraband was sent for Chemical examination to
FSL, Agra and after obtaining the report of the Chemical
Analyst, he submitted the charge-sheet against the accused. It
was admitted by PW7 that he did not record the statement of
any witness prior to submission of the charge-sheet because the
statement of the witnesses were already recorded by his
predecessor. The case property of this case was not produced
before PW7 at the time of deposition. PW7 however, denied the
suggestion that the investigation was not conducted by him as
per law and a false charge-sheet was submitted by him against
the accused.

6
8. PW5 Sri O.P. Taneja was the scientist, who chemically
examined the case property of this case which was sent to him
by learned Chief Judicial Magistrate. He admitted that the
quantity of the representative sample (4 grams) was insufficient
for detecting the actual percentage of morphine in it. The
recovered substance in the polythenes was sent to PW5 for
chemical examination. PW5 detected 5.4 percent morphine in
the said contraband. PW5 proved his report (Ext-Ka7). He said
that the contraband was received by him in sealed condition.
PW5 admitted that in Ext-Ka7 he did not mention that he did
receive the sample of seal alongwith the contraband. He
clarified that the mentioning of the words 'namoona ke anusar
(as per sample)' in his report itself revealed that the contraband
was found in sealed packet bearing the seal similar to the
sample of seal. He denied the suggestion of the defence that he
did not try to see that the seal on the relevant packet was similar
to the sample seal and that he did not examine the contraband
as per rules.
9. Since the incident occurred all of a sudden, therefore the
availability of public witness was a remote possibility. The
incident took place in the month of December at 5.30 P.M. in
the jungle, therefore, non-procurement of public witness (es)
did not do any bad to the prosecution story.
10. Learned counsel for the appellant contended that there
was non-compliance of Section 50 of N.D.P.S. Act. The said
argument carries no weight, in as much as, if a police officer

7
without any prior information as contemplated under the
provisions of N.D.P.S. Act makes a search or arrests a person in
the normal course of investigation into an offence of suspected
offence as provided under the provisions of Cr.P.C. and when
such search is completed at that stage, Section 50 of N.D.P.S.
Act would not be attracted and the question of complying with
the requirements thereunder would not arise. If during such
search or arrest there is a chance recovery of any narcotic drug
or psychotropic substance then the police officer, who is not
empowered should inform the empowered officer who should
thereafter proceed in accordance with the provisions of NDPS
Act. If he happens to be an empowered officer also, then from
that stage onwards, he should carry out the investigation in
accordance with the other provisions of the N.D.P.S. Act.
Since it was a chance recovery and police party had no prior
intimation that some person was carrying Narcotic Substance,
no prejudice was caused to the accused-appellant in not
complying with the directory provisions of the Act, as was held
by Hon'ble Apex Court in State of Punjab vs. Balbeer Singh,
1994 SCC (Cri) 634, at Page 638.
11. It was next argued by learned counsel for the appellant
that the superior police officer was not informed by the police
personnel, which argument was contrary to the evidence on
record, in as much as, it was evidenced that the information was
given to the senior police officer on wireless. Information was
also given to the family members of the accused. The
contraband was also weighed on the spot by using weighing

8
machine. A policeman brought the weighing machine from a
nearby shop.
12. It was also contended by learned counsel for the appellant
that link evidence was not produced by the prosecution. This
argument was also contrary to the evidence on record, in as
much as PW2 was the link evidence who took the
representative sample to FSL, Agra in sealed condition under
the authority of Chief Judicial Magistrate.
13. To recapitulate, PW1 said that he, alongwith other police
personnel apprehended the accused, who was in possession of
opium. No independent witness was available and therefore the
public witness could not be procured. The contraband found
from the possession of the accused smelt opium. It was black
coloured narcotic substance. The police personnel adjudged
the same to be opium on the basis of it's physical
characteristics. Constable Lokendra was sent to bring weighing
machine. The contraband was weighed. It weighed 228 gms.
Representative sample of 4 gms was taken. A recovery memo
was prepared which contained the signatures of the accused.
Accused was told about the offence which he committed. The
case was registered. The higher authorities of police were
informed on wireless. The contraband was taken to the police
station and was kept under the seal. The family members of the
accused were informed. The contraband was produced in court
at the time of deposition. The representative sample was sent to
FSL, Agra. In the cross-examination PW1 reiterated that the

9
memo of taking search of police personnel was prepared.
Memo of weighment of contraband was also prepared. A
Constable was sent to inform the family members of the
accused. Entry of the same was made in the general diary. PW1
was subjected to lengthy cross examination, but nothing
material came so as to suspect his testimony. PW2 was the link
evidence, who took the representative sample to FSL, Agra,
and got the same received there. He did not permit anybody to
touch the contraband. He proceeded from the police station at
around 12 noon for Agra. The same was entered in the general
diary. PW3 Constable Prem Singh supported PW1. He was one
of those police personnel who found opium in the possession
the accused. PW4 S.I. Zakir Hussain was the investigating
officer of the case. Forensic Science Laboratory, in its report,
revealed that the sample of contraband, which was sent to lab,
was opium. PW5 Sri O.P. Taneja, Joint Director, FSL Agra
stated that the FSL received a packet of representative sample.
The same was chemically examined and was found to be
opium. PW 6 Head Constable Gajraj Singh was a formal
witness, who proved chik F.I.R. (Ext.Ka8) and entries in G.D.
(Ext-Ka9, Ext-Ka10, Ext-Ka11 and Ext-Ka12). He also said
that the contraband was kept sealed in malkhana. PW7 S.O.
Surendra Singh Bisht conducted investigation at some length
and finally submitted charge sheet Ext-Ka 6 against the
accused. In this way, it was proved by the prosecution
witnesses that the mandatory provisions of the N.D.P.S. Act,
1985 were complied with.

10
14. Learned counsel for the accused appellant contended that
the accused was not a previous convict and therefore his past
conduct should be considered. No doubt, there is no indication
on record to show that the accused-appellant was a previous
convict, but this court is unable to help the appellant in view of
the fact that he was awarded minimum sentence by the trial
court. The amendment in Section 21 of N.D.P.S. Act was made
effective from 2.10.2001 and the present incident was of an
earlier date, therefore the benefit of amendment cannot be given
to the accused-appellant. The amendment in Section 42 of
N.D.P.S. Act 1985 was made effective from 2.10.2001. The
amendment in Section 21 was also carried out with effect from
2.10.2001, and the present incident took place on 2.12.1997,
almost three years before the amendments came into being,
therefore, the accused-appellant was not entitled to any benefit
arising out of those amendments.
15. The entire prosecution evidence was appropriately dealt
with by learned Sessions Judge, Dehradun, who committed no
mistake in correctly appreciating the evidence thus brought on
record. There is no illegality in the impugned judgment and
order. A different view is not possible to be taken in the
absence of any evidence to the contrary. No interference is thus
called for in the judgment rendered by learned court below.
16. Criminal appeal filed on behalf of the appellant is
dismissed. The conviction and sentence awarded to the
appellant is affirmed. The convict-appellant is on bail. His bail

11
is cancelled. He is directed to surrender forthwith before the
Court below to serve out the sentence, as was awarded to him
by the trial court.
17. Let a copy of this judgment alongwith lower court record
be sent to the trial court for causing the appellant to surrender
and sending him to prison to serve the remaining part of his
sentence.
(U.C. Dhyani, J.)
